backups.approach: From the Trinity Trailhead (~2,820 ft, at the end of Chiwawa River/Chiwawa Valley Road, Forest Road 6200, reached via Coles Corner and Hwy 207), pick up the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 and follow it upstream through forest for roughly 4 miles. Watch the left (west) side of the trail for an 'M' blazed/carved into a tree — this marks the unsigned, unmaintained sheepherder's path up to Massie Lake, and it's easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. Ford the Chiwawa River at this point (can run cold and pushy with snowmelt into early summer; trekking poles help, expect wet feet) and pick up the old sheep-drive trail, which climbs steeply via a mix of tree blazes and intermittent boot-track for about 2 miles to Massie Lake (about 5,900 ft), a clear trout-holding tarn with a couple of established campsites. There is essentially no reliable water between the river ford and the lake, so fill up at the Chiwawa. From Massie Lake, continue on the faint sheep/game-trail tread of the Massie Lake High Route, contouring northwest roughly 1.5 miles toward Pass No Pass, then leave that trail and turn uphill (climber's right) onto Massie Peak's broad west ridge. Follow the ridge crest east for a bit over a mile — talus and heather with a few short rock steps, generally Class 2 with brief Class 3 moves near the summit block — to the 7,533 ft summit. The main hazard throughout is route-finding: the sheepherder path disappears in places, blazes thin out above treeline, and the entire line beyond the Chiwawa River Trail is off-trail, unsigned, and easy to lose in flat light — bring a map/GPS track. Snow and ice can linger on shaded sections of the high route and ridge well into summer; many parties carry microspikes and a light ice axe for trips before mid-July.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the west ridge (Class 2-3, some loose rock underfoot) back to the point where you gained it from the Massie Lake High Route, rejoin that faint tread and follow it back southeast to Massie Lake, then descend the steep sheepherder path back down to the Chiwawa River ford and out the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 to Trinity Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route — there are no fixed anchors reported on Massie Peak's west ridge or the approach gully, consistent with its Class 2-3 scrambling character. The trickiest part of the descent is simply staying on the correct (badly faded) line: the sheep trail is easy to lose both up in the high-route traverse and on the steep drop back to the river, and a mistaken line can dead-end in cliff bands or brush. Some parties instead continue past Massie Lake and pick a 'route of least resistance' down open slopes directly to Buck Creek Trail when linking Massie Peak with neighboring summits (Mount Cleator, Helmet Butte, Liberty Cap) on a multi-day loop, but for a straightforward out-and-back on the West Route, reversing the ascent line described above is the standard descent.
backups.bail: Retreat by reversing the ascent line back toward Massie Lake and down to the Chiwawa River crossing, then out the Chiwawa River Trail to Trinity Trailhead. No technical rope work is typically required to bail, but parties who wander off the standard line have encountered short 4th-class cliff bands that require careful, deliberate downclimbing.

climate.typical: High country here holds snow into July; late July through September is the reliable snow-free window for the West Ridge scramble. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in the Glacier Peak Wilderness high country in summer — start early and plan to be off the exposed ridge crest by early afternoon.

bySeason.fall: Access can extend into September in dry years, but shortening days, early snow, and dried-up water sources raise the stakes.
bySeason.spring: Still snow-covered and avalanche-prone; not a typical season for this scramble.
bySeason.summer: Prime season, especially August; expect biting insects at Massie Lake and possible afternoon thunderstorms.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible — remote, unplowed access road and heavy snowpack.

approach_variants.name: Chiwawa River Trail to the sheepherder's path and Massie Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the Chiwawa valley, fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit and follow the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 upstream through forest, watching the west side of the tread for the marker described below. Ford the river at that point — it can run thigh-deep and swift with early-season snowmelt, so cross in the morning when flows are lowest — and pick up the old sheep-drive path, which climbs steeply on a mix of axe and burn blazes and intermittent boot track to Massie Lake. There is essentially no reliable water between the ford and the lake. From the lake the faint sheep and game tread of the high route contours northwest toward the pass ahead; leave it and turn uphill onto the peak's broad west ridge.
approach_variants.season: The high country here is typically not fully snow-free until mid to late July; shaded sections of the high route and ridge hold snow and ice well into summer.

approach_variants.baseFinding: TWO THINGS FACING EACH OTHER ACROSS THE TRAIL MARK IT: A LARGE BOULDER JUTTING IN FROM THE EAST, AND AN 'M' WITH AN ARROW CARVED INTO A TREE ON THE WEST. The boulder is what you actually see first. There is no sign and no trail number, and the path it marks is an old sheep-drive route that is easy to walk straight past. The river is forded immediately below the junction, with piled driftwood the only help across, so the ford and the carved letter go together. The serious trap here is a decoy: a false set of markers — a boulder in the bank and logs and arrows suggesting the lake — has existed roughly a mile short of the real junction, and a party that took it spent hours bushwhacking up the wrong hillside and came out on the ridge high above the lake. So do not settle for arrows alone; you want the boulder and the carved 'M' opposite one another, and cairns have since been built on both sides of the trail at the true crossing. Above the ford a steep, poorly-marked boot track climbs to the lake on axe and burn blazes that thin out with height. From the lake the faint high route contours away; leave it and turn uphill onto the broad west ridge, the only named feature near that decision being a shoulder around 6,420 ft.

climbing_route.label: Broad west ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Leave the Massie Lake High Route short of Pass No Pass and turn uphill (climber's right) onto Massie Peak's broad west ridge, then follow the ridge crest east for a bit over a mile to the 7,533 ft summit — talus and heather with a few short rock steps, generally Class 2 with brief Class 3 moves near the summit block. Route-finding is the main hazard: blazes thin out above treeline and the line is unsigned and easy to lose in flat light, so carry a map/GPS track. Snow and ice linger on shaded sections of the ridge well into summer; many parties carry microspikes and a light ice axe before mid-July.

bivy.name: Massie Lake basin
bivy.notes: This is the climbing camp for Massie Peak and effectively the only one, because everything above it is dry and everything below it is a long way down. From the Trinity trailhead the Buck Creek trail runs a mile and a half to the junction, the Chiwawa River trail carries on up the valley and crosses the river on a bridge, and about three miles along it the Massie Lake trail turns off and climbs roughly two miles to the lake, at about 5,900 feet. THAT LAST STRETCH IS THE DIFFICULTY AND IT IS NOT A TRAIL IN ANY USEFUL SENSE. It is an unsigned and unmaintained old sheep driveway, steep, brushy and lost altogether in places, and the standard complaint about this lake is the amount of bushwhacking involved in reaching it. Expect to lose the line more than once and to be pushing through vegetation on the steepest part of the day. From camp the west route on Massie Peak goes on open slopes above the basin and is a scramble rather than a climb. The reward for the thrash is genuine solitude and good fishing; the register-level traffic here is a fraction of what the Buck Creek Pass side sees. Season is roughly mid-July into early October, later than a lake this height would suggest because the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable all season. This is the last certain water on the climb and the reason to camp here rather than higher: the slopes and benches above the basin run on snowmelt only and are dry by August in an ordinary year. Fill completely before going up. Treat it, though the shoreline sees very little use.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the Trinity trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book in advance. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at Trinity. Camp back from the shoreline and on existing bare ground; this is a small basin and it marks easily. Carry a stove — summer fire restrictions on this dry east side are routine and often total.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake for one or two parties. There is nothing developed, nothing signed and no toilet, and the basin is small — but it is also so little visited that competition for space is not a realistic worry.

bivy.name: Trinity trailhead roadhead
bivy.notes: The staging point, and it is recorded because the drive is the part of this trip that most often goes wrong. In a normal year the Chiwawa River road runs about twenty-two miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, with the last stretch rough gravel genuinely unsuited to low clearance, and arriving at the end of it late and tired is how parties end up starting the walk in badly. From the roadhead a short section of closed road leads onto the Buck Creek trail, and the junction where the Chiwawa River trail branches right for Massie is a mile and a half in. THE ROAD IS SHUT ABOVE ATKINSON FLAT under a storm-damage order running into 2027, with the 2026 fire closure sitting over the same corridor on top of it, and while that stands there is no legal way to drive to this roadhead at all. When the road is open again, expect it to remain the fragile part of any plan here: it has been damaged repeatedly, it carries no through traffic to justify quick repair, and the trailhead is far enough up it that a single washout removes the whole approach.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is close by and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap anywhere at this end of the road. Fill everything here, since the valley trail above is good for water and the climb to the lake is not.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is taken from the register here — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit including stock. Fire restrictions bite hard on this side from midsummer and commonly ban all open flame including in existing rings.
bivy.capacity: A gravel parking area at the end of the public road with room to sleep in a vehicle. It is a roadhead, not a campground — no fee site, no tables, no toilet you should count on. The developed campgrounds strung along the Chiwawa River road below it are the proper drive-in option and are recorded in the Entiat and Holden file rather than repeated here.

bivy.name: The Chiwawa River trail camps above the bridge
bivy.notes: These are the first-night camps for a party that has driven a long way, or the last-night camps for one walking out, and on this approach both cases are common. The river bridge where the Buck Creek trail crosses is the usual spot and is the obvious place to stop, being flat, sheltered and on good water. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the Massie Lake turn is unsigned and the driveway above it is steep and vague — that is ground you want to meet in the morning with fresh legs and a full day, not at dusk. The valley walking below is gentle and fast, so a party that gets away from the road in the afternoon can be here comfortably. THE ROAD CLOSURE CHANGES THE ARITHMETIC ENTIRELY. With the Chiwawa River road shut above Atkinson Flat, Trinity is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns the walk to these camps into a long day on its own or a bike shuttle, and turns the trip as a whole from two nights into three or four.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is alongside for this whole stretch and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is where the approach is generous with water, and it is worth knowing because the climb to Massie Lake is the steep, hot, brushy part and there is nothing dependable on it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit from the Trinity trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal below the high country in existing rings outside a burn ban, but the Chiwawa valley is dry and bans are the norm from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the timber along the valley floor, including good ground where the trail crosses the river on the bridge. One or two parties each, nothing developed, and rarely anyone else there.

bivy.name: The benches above Massie Lake — no established camp
bivy.notes: Recorded honestly: Massie Peak is a day objective from the lake and there is no practical reason to sleep higher. The scramble from the basin is short enough that the only argument for going up is to be on the crest at first light, and the cost is carrying water two thousand feet and sleeping exposed with nothing to shelter behind. The one situation where these benches genuinely earn their place is the traverse northwest on the old sheepherder's line toward Pass No Pass and the Buck Creek Pass country, which runs two and a half to three miles on faint stock and game tracks that come and go, and which a party will not finish in the same day they climb the peak. If you are doing that, sleeping high on the way out makes sense. If you are climbing Massie and walking back down the driveway, it does not. Either way, do not plan on finding water and do not plan on finding a flat, cleared spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. By August there is usually nothing at all above the lake, and a party sleeping up here is carrying every drop from the basin below. This is the single most common way to get the trip wrong.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at Trinity. No fires this high — carry a stove. The ground is thin subalpine turf that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
bivy.capacity: None established. There is open ground on the benches and in the meadows above the lake where a small party could put down a tent, but nothing has been built, nothing is marked, and nobody camps here as a matter of course. That is worth saying plainly rather than inventing a site.
